definition: An inauthentic text is a computer-generated expository document meant to appear as genuine, but which is actually meaningless.
details: Frequently they are created in order to be intermixed with genuine documents and thus manipulate the results of search engines, as with Spam blogs. They are also carried along in email in order to fool spam filters by giving the spam the superficial characteristics of legitimate text. Sometimes nonsensical documents are created with computer assistance for humorous effect, as with Dissociated press or Flarf poetry. They have also been used to challenge the veracity of a publication—MIT students submitted papers generated by a computer program called SCIgen to a conference, where they were initially accepted. This led the students to claim that the bar for submissions was too low. With the amount of computer generated text outpacing the ability of people to humans to curate it, there needs some means of distinguishing between the two. Yet automated approaches to determining absolutely whether a text is authentic or not face intrinsic challenges of semantics. Noam Chomsky coined the phrase "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" giving an example of grammatically correct, but semantically incoherent sentence; some will point out that in certain contexts one could give this sentence (or any phrase) meaning. The first group to use the expression in this regard can be found below from Indiana University. Their work explains in detail an attempt to detect inauthentic texts and identify pernicious problems of inauthentic texts in cyberspace. The site has a means of submitting text that assesses, based on supervised learning, whether a corpus is inauthentic or not. Many users have submitted incorrect types of data and have correspondingly commented on the scores. This application is meant for a specific kind of data; therefore, submitting, say, an email, will not return a meaningful score.

explainer.lead: Computer-generated expository documents designed to look genuine but that are actually meaningless. They matter because they contaminate search results, email filters, and the perceived trustworthiness of published material.

tiers.eli5: It's like a page of writing that looks like a real essay but says nothing of substance, made by a machine so it blends in with real documents.
tiers.practitioner: Spammers use them to give junk email the superficial shape of legitimate text and to pollute search-engine indexes via spam blogs. A pitfall is that filtering on fluency alone fails, since the text is deliberately well-formed.
tiers.paperLevel: Informally defined by intent and effect rather than by a formal property: a generated document with the surface characteristics of expository prose but no genuine content. No single accepted detection criterion exists.

explainer.example: A spam blog fills itself with machine-generated meaningless paragraphs so its links appear among legitimate results; a spam email trails similar text to slip past filters.
